watch_out: Ninemile Saddle (~mile 4.5) is a narrow, roughly ten-foot-wide knife-edge ridge crossing steep, rock-filled gullies on both sides -- use caution in wind or when wet/icy.
Mountain goats frequent the summit area and can approach closely; keep well clear and do not feed or approach them.
Water is scarce along the entire route -- carry all you need.
South-facing slopes between Alpine Lookout and Merritt Lake see significant avalanche activity in spring and are not suitable for travel without avalanche-aware routefinding/gear in that season.
pro_tips: The first ~1.6 miles on Round Mountain Trail #1529 up to the Nason Ridge Trail junction are the steepest part of the hike; most of the elevation gain happens early.
Alpine Lookout is one of the earliest high points on Nason Ridge to lose its snow, making it a good target when higher Cascades peaks are still snowed in.
The lookout is staffed by a Forest Service volunteer/employee most summers -- visitors are generally welcome to chat but should respect it as an active duty station.
A fun, moderate way to reach Amphitheater's summit plateau roped-up rather than via the pure scramble West Route
Several pitches offer solid 5.5 climbing rather than loose scrambling — pick the cleaner rock where route-finding allows

before.approach: Two common trailheads reach the base: (1) Andrews Creek Trailhead (Trail 504) — from Winthrop, take Hwy 20 to County Road 1213/West Chewuch Road, drive ~6 miles to Forest Road 51, continue ~22 miles to the trailhead at the end of the pavement (3,050 ft). Hike via Andrews Pass and the Boundary Trail to Upper Cathedral Lake (roughly 7 hours for a loaded backpacking pace). (2) Chewuch River Trail/Thirtymile Trailhead — a longer approach (about 20 miles and ~4,900 ft gain to Upper Cathedral Lake), also joining near Cathedral Pass. Most parties backpack in and camp at or near Upper Cathedral Lake (~7,380 ft) before a summit day.

From the Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail past the Colchuck Lake junction (do not turn off), then leave the trail to bushwhack and cross Mountaineer Creek (a notorious slide-alder slope is best avoided via nearby talus). Snow is typically encountered around 4,700 ft; continue to the base of the north face couloir.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late May to early June, while the couloir holds consolidated spring snow and the trailhead road has opened

May.reason: The trailhead road typically opens in May and late-month freeze-thaw firms the 35-50 degree couloir; start early before the sun softens it.

July.reason: The couloir melts out into loose rock, brush and moats, rockfall increases in the narrow slot, and the Colchuck Glacier descent opens up.

June.reason: Early June still has continuous snow in the narrows; as the month goes on the couloir thins, ice shows at the constrictions and the exit gets wet.

April.reason: The trailhead road is usually still gated, adding miles of snowy walking, and the couloir can hold unconsolidated or avalanche-prone snow.

what_to_bring: Helmet - rockfall/icefall risk in the couloir
Glacier travel gear for the Colchuck Glacier descent
Extra layers - the couloir is often shaded and cold
ice axes and crampons — single or double axes, for the couloir
pro_tips: Best climbed while the couloir still holds consolidated spring snow, before it melts out to loose rock and scree later in summer.
If frozen after a freeze-thaw cycle, the couloir can go to neve or ice - budget for a slower, more technical ascent.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with August generally the sweet spot

July.reason: Early-season entry to the window; glacier snow coverage is firmer and may still bridge some crevasses, but approach brush can still be wet and lush

August.reason: Most stable weather window of the season; brush more manageable and glacier generally passable, though afternoon thunderstorms are possible

September.reason: Can offer stable spells and cooler temps, but crevasses are more open late season

pro_tips: Plan for a slow, brushy approach — it is the crux of the trip
Standard glacier precautions on the summit icecap

before.approach: From the FS 3160 road-end parking (roughly 48.957°N, 121.851°W, reached via Canyon Creek Road/FS 31 then FS 3160 as noted above), the route follows an unmaintained but well-worn boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail, just a heavily used user track — that climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft of gain to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake sitting in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first pitch is the steepest sustained grade of the day. Skirt the lake along its east/left shore (best flat campsites are on the far side, useful if splitting the trip). Beyond the lake the trail fades into intermittent boot-path and cairns through meadows and heather benches; keep left (east) up the basin rim toward a broad knoll around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block — this stretch accounts for most of the remaining ~900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 mi one-way (matching the ~5.9 km round trip). From the 6,066 ft knoll, drop slightly and traverse north across a rocky/heather bowl toward the base of Bearpaw's summit block; the final approximately 300 ft to the 6,091 ft summit is easy class 2-3 scrambling on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure in the last pitch. Church Lake is the last reliable water source — carry water from there for the upper mountain. There is no maintained tread past the lake, so route-finding by cairns and boot-path is necessary, and in early/mid-season lingering snow on the steep initial slope above the lake and in the summit gullies can require an ice axe and caution; parties often find snow patches into July on shaded sections.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-August through September, once the high country has melted out

July.reason: Snow lingers late at this elevation; route-finding and footing are harder, and some slopes may still be snow-covered

June.reason: Deep snow still covers approach slopes and the summit scramble; not in season

August.reason: Scramble season is established once high country has melted; best combination of dry rock/heather and stable weather

October.reason: Border-country weather deteriorates and early snow can return, closing the short seasonal window

September.reason: Continuation of the short clear scramble window before fall weather moves in

watch_out: The final summit move is on an unprotectable friction slab — a fall here would be serious.
The upper-mountain scree is unusually loose, like fine gravel rolling over sand, even by North Cascades standards.
There are no reliable water sources once you leave Willow Creek.
pro_tips: Go in late spring/early summer while snow still covers the upper basin — it firms up the ground and is faster and more secure than the loose scree found later in summer.
Stay on the north side of Willow Creek on the lower approach to minimize brush-fighting.
Many parties boost the leader onto the crux summit slab with a shoulder stand rather than attempting to free-climb the unprotected 5.7-5.8 move.
before.approach: Park in a highway pullout on SR-20 about 3.5 miles east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 4,320 ft elevation). Descend to and cross Early Winters Creek, then head up into the Willow Creek valley, staying on the north side of the creek. The first ~3/4 mile up the valley is steep and can be very brushy in summer. Around 5,000 ft the slope eases; continue up loose/open terrain into the upper basin near 7,000 ft, then traverse a loose scree or snow slope for about 400 ft to reach the saddle on the west ridge (~7,400 ft).

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late May to June, when snow still covers the loose slope to the west-ridge saddle and the Willow Creek brush is low

May.reason: Firm spring snow covers the loose basin and the slope to the saddle; start early before the snow softens and slides.

July.reason: Snow melts back, exposing more loose talus, and the lower Willow Creek slope gets brushier; the ridge itself is dry.

June.reason: Snow still bridges most of the scree to the saddle and the summit slab is usually dry; crampons and an axe help on the upper slope.

April.reason: SR-20 is usually still gated for spring clearing; once open, the deep Willow Creek basin carries real avalanche risk.

August.reason: The 400-ft slope to the saddle becomes loose kitty-litter scree, the brush is at its worst and the open ridge is hot.

October.reason: Cold, short days and early snow on the friction slab; SR-20 can close at short notice with the first big storms.

September.reason: Still a loose scree slog to the saddle, though cooler; fresh snow on the summit slab makes the unprotected move dangerous.

before.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb about 10 ft to a rappel anchor and rappel the short friction slab, then downclimb/scramble back to the top of the lower chimney and rappel (existing webbing/anchors reported) to the ridge below. From there, descend the class 2 west ridge back to the upper basin, retrace the scree/snow traverse, and descend the Willow Creek drainage (loose, brushy) back to the SR-20 pullout. A 30m rope is sufficient for both rappels.

before.approach: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate and walk (or mountain-bike) the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about 7 miles to the boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes, which starts roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake, staying near the inlet — straying left leads into cliff bands.
watch_out: Straying left (north) of the inlet path to upper Hardscrabble Lake leads into cliff bands
The route is now a roughly 25-mile round trip due to the Dingford Creek gate — budget time, food, and water accordingly
The gully to the col above Hardscrabble Lakes can hold snow/ice into early summer
what_to_bring: Overnight gear if camping at Hardscrabble Lakes
Extra water for the long road-walk approach

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to mid-September, after the gully to the col melts out and before autumn snow returns to the granite slab

July.reason: The upper gully and col melt out through the month; early July can still hold a snow patch in the gully.

June.reason: The road walk is clear, but the gully to the col and the north-slope slab still hold snow that needs an axe and often crampons.

August.reason: Snow-free gully and dry granite slab give the easiest travel; start early for the long bike or walk on the gated road.

October.reason: First snows ice the open slab on the north slope and daylight barely covers the 14-mile road round trip plus the climb.

September.reason: Dry route, cooler temperatures for the long road approach, and fewer bugs at the lakes; days are noticeably shorter.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to mid-September, once the gullies above Big Snow Lake have mostly melted but the couloir can still hold firm snow

July.reason: The NW couloir usually still holds firm snow over the loose rock, while the lower brush and gullies have opened up.

June.reason: Steep gullies above Big Snow Lake are full of snow and the lakes may still be frozen; crampons and an axe are essential.

August.reason: Gullies are largely melted out and route-finding past Snowflake Lake is easiest, though the couloir turns to loose talus.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas on the chutes, short days for a long off-trail route, and a remote setting for self-rescue.

September.reason: Dry, loose chutes and cooler weather; any remaining snow in the gullies can be hard and icy in the morning.

pro_tips: Carry a GPS track for the Myrtle Lake to Big Snow Lake off-trail section — the correct gully is easy to miss
Camping at Myrtle or Big Snow Lake breaks the long day into two more comfortable ones
Traverse right around Snowflake Lake to link into the correct summit gully

watch_out: loose rock
remoteness / self-rescue distance
afternoon thunderstorms
pro_tips: Tag it on the same trip as Monument and Lago
Watch for lingering snow on shaded aspects early season

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with late July-August offering the driest, most reliable talus conditions

July.reason: Early July can still have residual snow patches; conditions typically firm up to match the mid-July start of best-season

June.reason: (spring = snow-covered), the ridge and approach basins likely still hold lingering snow, adding routefinding difficulty and exposure on the Class 3 sections

August.reason: Prime in summer - driest continental NE Cascades conditions and most stable weather window

September.reason: Still within the best-season and generally stable per climate data, but shorter daylight and higher chance of an early-season weather change late in the month

what_to_bring: Green Trails map No. 49 (Washington Pass) / No. 50 (Mt. Logan)
Overnight camping gear for Wing Lake (or plan a very long single push)
Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking; wilderness permit if camping in the Park
Extra layers — the ridge is exposed and can be windy/cold even in summer
watch_out: Extremely loose rock low on the ridge — test every hold and expect some 'Jenga-like' blocks, especially near the summit tower.
A lingering snowfield/small glacier crossing below the col may demand crampons well into the season.
The South Ridge descent gully is loose and tedious and has caught out descending parties as much as the climb itself.
before.descent_text: From the summit, work down and south toward the South Ridge route, using one rappel or a down-climb to get below the initial band of rock, then continuing south to the south col. From there the descent follows the South Ridge's loose, cairned gully (described by multiple parties as tedious and 'choss'-prone) back down to snow slopes and Wing Lake. Some parties glissade the snow lower down early in the season.
pro_tips: Follow the hogsback moraine wide right from Wing Lake, then traverse back left to the notch, to stay on more stable terrain and avoid the steepest snow.
Expect the worst rock low on the ridge — quality improves noticeably the higher you climb.
Most parties simul-climb the 3rd/4th-class sections and belay only the low-5th steps, which speeds the route considerably.
before.approach: As for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass/Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, via Heather Pass and Lewis Lake to a camp at Wing Lake (~6,900 ft). From camp, ascend snow (a small permanent snowfield/mini-glacier can persist below the col into September) toward the low point in the Northeast Ridge — following the hogsback moraine wide right and then traversing back left to the notch is reported to stay on more stable ground than a direct line.

The approach follows the same trailhead-in as the standard route — Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) from Holden Village to the Holden Lake Trail junction, then up to Holden Lake (5,278') and Holden Pass (6,360') for high camp — but instead of angling onto the Mary Green Glacier itself, continue on benches and talus/heather to climber's right (east/north side) of the glacier. This adds roughly another 3 hours and substantial elevation gain beyond Holden Pass to reach the base of the Northeast Buttress/Face around 8,350'. Total gain ends up close to the standard Mary Green line's, since both leave the same camp and finish on the same summit. Water sources match the standard approach (Holden Lake, Holden Pass); above the pass, plan on carrying what you need since there's little reliable water on the buttress approach itself. Expect loose rock and routefinding on the benches, and — because this line stays right of the glacier on rock rather than crossing snow/ice — less exposure to crevasse hazard but more exposure to rockfall and unconsolidated talus underfoot.
before.descent_text: The straightforward descent reverses down to the Mary Green Glacier and follows the standard route's descent: down-climb the summit ridge/rock rib, use the fixed rappel stations through the class 3–4 band (about four rappels with a 60m rope, 8mm lines are common), cross the moat, and descend the glacier to Holden Pass camp — see the Mary Green Glacier route's descent notes for full detail on that shared lower section. Parties combining this face with a full three-summit traverse instead descend from the Southwest Peak via ledges onto the Isella Glacier's upper snowfields, traverse to the Southeast (Holden) Ridge, climb a short ~5.7 chimney, and then make a single rappel from the col back down onto the Mary Green Glacier before rejoining the standard glacier descent to camp. Either way, expect loose rock on the upper buttress and ridge sections and take care with rope management around the gendarmes and notches.

July.reason: Early part of the Best Jul-Sep window; some residual snow possible early month but conditions generally climbable

June.reason: Spring is Snowbound; approach gullies and basin likely still hold significant snow, adding difficulty and avalanche/wet-slide concern

August.reason: Core of the best season; driest, most stable rock conditions for the Class 4 climbing

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; climate field indicates fall cooling toward winter, with new snow likely making the loose Class 4 terrain more hazardous

September.reason: Still within the best season but fall is Cool - shorter days and earlier storms possible

watch_out: pulling loose blocks off the face
rockfall triggered by the party, especially onto climbers below on the rappel line
the exposed, rotten summit
afternoon storms

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August the most reliable month

July.reason: Late-July start of the window; lingering snowfields on approach slopes and higher creek flows are possible of spring snow lingering

August.reason: Driest, most stable east-side Cascades conditions; summer is the Best season

September.reason: Still generally dry but the window is short ('Short window' for fall) before autumn storms and early snow move in

pro_tips: Camp at Entiat Meadows to break the ~30-mile round trip into 2-3 days rather than a single huge day
Pair with Mount Fernow or Seven Fingered Jack from the same high camp - all three summits share the Fernow-Buckskin-Jack cirque
A mountain bike can save real time on the road approach if the seasonal gate below the trailhead is still closed
Stay below the ridge crest near the top of the east ridge to avoid cornices and loose gendarmes
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, follow the east ridge back down to roughly 7,200-7,900 ft, then drop off the ridge onto the same south-facing rib/gully used on the way up, picking your way down through loose scree and heather (roughly 3,000 ft of scree plus slick heather) back to the upper Entiat Meadows camp/trail. From there it's a straightforward but long reverse of the Entiat River Trail #1400 (roughly 14.5-15 miles) back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no technical rappelling involved — rope and anchor gear are not part of a normal summer ascent. The scree and heather are noticeably looser and more slippery on the way down than going up, and the burned, faint upper stretch of trail plus any deadfall-choked side paths are the main route-finding hazards on the way out; give yourself enough daylight given the ~15-mile, 5,000 ft round-trip scale of the day.
watch_out: steep, icy snow and cornices on the ridge into June/early July
heavy mosquitoes in Entiat Meadows through midsummer
faint boot path above the meadows - easy to end up on a brushier or looser line than necessary

before.approach: From the Dingford Creek gate, walk or bike the closed Middle Fork road (FR 56) about 7.7 miles to its end at Hardscrabble Horse Camp; bikes go no farther. Burnt Boot stands across the Middle Fork to the south, and its north ridge drops straight from the summit to the river near 3,100 ft. There is no bridge here (the next one is at Pedro Camp, near mile 13), so head upstream from the horse camp toward Hardscrabble Creek and ford the river; it can run cold and thigh-deep in July, and logs across it may not reach. From the south bank it is cross-country up steep forest and brush on the ridge to the base of its steepest granite, where the roped climbing starts. There is no trail or established line off the valley floor.

July.reason: Prime season once gully snow has melted out; long daylight for the full ~7-hr day

August.reason: Driest, most stable conditions; also the busiest month, so midweek starts help avoid Liberty Bell overflow traffic

September.reason: Cool, stable weather and fewer parties, but shorter daylight window narrows the margin for the alpine start

pro_tips: Pair Concord with Lexington Tower and/or Liberty Bell for an efficient multi-summit day.
Keep the rack light to move fast over the short pitches.
Watch for loose rock on ledges and below other parties.
Pitch 2's crux is essentially unprotectable, insecure climbing on huge huecos — commit rather than hunting for gear; pitch 3's crack takes a #3 cam.

watch_out: The balancy move left on P2 to reach the second crack is described as committing — know it's coming before you commit to the first crack
before.descent_text: The route rejoins the Beckey Route line near its top; descend via the standard two single-rope rappels off chain/bolted anchors down to the Liberty-Concord notch.

watch_out: Expect other parties intending the Beckey Route to end up on this line by mistake — be ready to help with directions or route-finding
before.descent_text: The route ends in easy fourth-class ground just below the summit, so use the normal Liberty Bell descent. From the top, retrace the ridge past the short slabby step, then follow the tree-filled gully east to the first bolted rappel station. A short series of single-rope rappels from fixed anchors, easily done with a 60 m rope, puts you in the Liberty-Concord notch at the top of the Beckey Gully. Scramble down the gully, taking care not to knock rocks onto parties below, and follow the trail back to the Blue Lakes trailhead.

before.watch_out:
South Arete provides less technical but more exposed line up the peak
Sustained exposure on buttress terrain with serious consequences for falls
Weather exposure creates hazard; electrical activity on exposed terrain
Loose rock on mixed terrain sections creates rockfall hazard
Descent route-finding can be challenging in low visibility

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June–September; south-southwest aspect clears early and holds condition later than shadier SEWS routes — described as 'nearly year-round' once SR-20 is open in low-snow years

May.reason: SR-20 typically still closed or only just reopening

July.reason: Reliable dry rock season, also the peak-traffic period

June.reason: South-southwest aspect clears early; pass-opening timing varies year to year

October.reason: Snow/moisture risk rising ahead of SR-20's seasonal closure

September.reason: Sunny aspect holds good condition later into the season than shadier routes

before.approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (elev. ~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-built Blue Lake Trail (Trail #314) as it climbs gently through subalpine fir and larch forest, switchbacking up open slabs with good views back at the highway. After roughly 1.3-1.5 miles and about 1,000 ft of gain, watch for a minor stream crossing/drainage coming down from the basin below the Early Winter Spires — this is well before Blue Lake itself, which lies another mile-plus further on the maintained trail. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the climbers' boot path (cairned but braided in spots) that works up through granite slabs and heather benches, then continues up open talus and boulder country roughly parallel to the stream, which is a reliable water source through most of the season lower down but disappears into talus higher up — fill up before leaving it. Continue up this climbers' trail, angling toward the southwestern corner/toe of South Early Winter Spire (the right-hand, southernmost of the two spires, before the saddle). Expect roughly another 1,000 ft of gain from where you leave the maintained trail to reach the base of the route at the level of the North/South spire saddle, for a total of about 2.5 hours and up to ~2,000 ft of gain from the car. The path is mostly straightforward but loses definition on the upper talus and slab benches — trend toward the obvious southwest corner of the spire rather than chasing any single cairn line, and take care on the granite slabs low down when wet or covered in old snow, which can persist into early summer in shaded gullies.
pro_tips: P1's 5.5 crux has two options: right via a slab traverse to a small tree, or left across a short friction-slab finger traverse — worth trying whichever suits your party's strengths.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: May, in the weeks after the North Cascades Highway opens, while the couloir still holds continuous snow

May.reason: The highway opens and deep, firm snow fills the couloir to the top; start early before the sun softens the southwest-facing slope.

July.reason: The couloir melts out to loose class 3-4 rubble with rockfall from above; only the lowest snow remains.

June.reason: Snow thins quickly, and in a light year the upper couloir melts out to loose rock steps by mid-June.

April.reason: The North Cascades Highway is usually still closed for the winter, and the couloir is avalanche terrain under spring storm snow.

August.reason: A dry gully of loose rock with steady rockfall; climb the neighbouring rock routes instead.

what_to_bring: Avalanche awareness for the approach slopes in spring
ice axe and crampons — snow-filled sections

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through September, with July-August the most reliable window for snow-free rock.

July.reason: Season typically opens as snow clears from the approach and ridge; matches start of best season.

August.reason: Driest, most stable rock and weather of the season, though afternoon thunderstorms remain a known hazard.

October.reason: Past the usual season: cold temps, shorter daylight, and potential early snowfall increase risk on exposed fourth-class terrain.

September.reason: Stable, cooler weather with fewer thunderstorms, but shorter days and possible early-season snow late in the month.

before.descent_text: Because the South Ridge is cliffed-out on multiple sides, parties descend by downclimbing and rappelling the same south-side line used on the ascent rather than walking off. From the summit block, the first rappel drops off a fixed station just below the top — parties describe a single old, not-fully-confidence-inspiring bolt/pin anchor here, so back it up with a cam or nut if you have any doubt — down past the 5.3-5.6 friction slab crux to a ledge. From there, most parties make one further rappel through a band of loose rock and boulders to a notch where the anchor is natural: a sling around a large wedged chockstone (some parties have refreshed this with a new sling and rap ring). A single 60m rope rappelled doubled (~30m per pitch) is generally sufficient, but at least one party found the rope only just reached the next station, so treat 60m as a minimum, knot your rope ends, and expect some parties to break the descent into three shorter rappels instead of two depending on the exact gully line and rope length carried. After the last rappel, downclimb and plunge-step the loose gully below the rockfall zone back onto the ascent talus, then retrace the approach through Temple Canyon, Tamarack Meadows, and the climbers' path back to Nada Lake and the Snow Lakes Trail. Wear a helmet throughout the descent — the gully channels loose rock kicked down by parties above.
watch_out: The crux slab move is protected by only one old bolt — inspect it before weighting and back it up with gear if you can.
Loose blocks litter the ridge and gully below the summit — helmets on, and stay alert to parties above or below.
This is a very long day even for fit parties (14+ hours car-to-car has been reported) — start pre-dawn and set a firm turnaround time.
